overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of the hard problem of consciousness and the explanatory gap. You'll be asked about Nagel's "what it is like," Levine's explanatory gap, Chalmers's easy and hard problems, the zombie argument, and the knowledge argument.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: What does Nagel's bat example show, according to his argument?

options.html: That bats lack conscious experience of any kind
options.text: That bats lack conscious experience of any kind
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nagel chooses bats because they are clearly conscious but very unlike us.

options.html: That what experience is like is tied to a point of view
options.text: That what experience is like is tied to a point of view
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Imagining behaving as a bat tells you what it would be like for you, not for a bat.

options.html: That echolocation can't be described by physics
options.text: That echolocation can't be described by physics
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Physics can describe echolocation. What it leaves out is what echolocating is like for the bat.

options.html: That physicalism has been proved to be false
options.text: That physicalism has been proved to be false
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nagel concludes that we don't understand how physicalism could be true, not that it's false.

forms.stemHtml: Levine grants that pain may be identical to a neural state. What does he say is still missing?

options.html: Evidence that the neural state causes pain behavior
options.text: Evidence that the neural state causes pain behavior
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The causal role is what the physical story explains well.

options.html: A proof that the pain is nonphysical
options.text: A proof that the pain is nonphysical
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Levine allows that materialism may be true. His gap is in explanation.

options.html: An account of why that state feels the way it does
options.text: An account of why that state feels the way it does
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is the explanatory gap: the identity, even if true, isn't made intelligible.

options.html: A way to measure pain in other people
options.text: A way to measure pain in other people
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Levine's point concerns explanation, not measurement.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are easy problems, in Chalmers's sense? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Explaining how a system reports its internal states
options.text: Explaining how a system reports its internal states
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Reportability is a function explained by a mechanism.

options.html: Explaining how attention selects some information
options.text: Explaining how attention selects some information
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The focus of attention is on Chalmers's list of easy problems.

options.html: Explaining how a system discriminates between stimuli
options.text: Explaining how a system discriminates between stimuli
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Discrimination is a cognitive function.

options.html: Explaining why any processing is accompanied by experience
options.text: Explaining why any processing is accompanied by experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the hard problem.

options.html: Explaining why tasting coffee feels like something
options.text: Explaining why tasting coffee feels like something
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Why an experience feels like anything is the hard problem.

forms.stemHtml: In the zombie argument, which step moves from a claim about what we can think to a claim about what could be?

options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This premise is only about what we can coherently think.

options.html: What is conceivable is therefore possible
options.text: What is conceivable is therefore possible
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This step bridges conceivability and possibility, and it's where many replies aim.
Sorry, that's incorrect. This is the conclusion, drawn from the possibility of zombies.

options.html: A zombie behaves as a conscious human does
options.text: A zombie behaves as a conscious human does
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's part of what a zombie is, not a step of the argument.

forms.stemHtml: What is the name for Jackson's argument that a scientist who knows all the physical facts about color vision still learns something new on first seeing red? Enter two words.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Jackson concludes that not all facts are physical.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Jackson's Mary case is the knowledge argument.

title: The Explanatory Gap
